source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: Gives UCB1 with a regret bound that is logarithmic in n for any finite n, not only in the limit. Builds on Lai and Robbins (1985), whose bound says the number of pulls of a bad arm must grow like ln n divided by a KL distance.
numbers: Rewards in [0,1]. Lower bound E[T_j(n)] >= (ln n)/D(p_j||p*) asymptotically. UCB1 index is the mean plus sqrt(2 ln n / n_j).
limits: Hoeffding-based bound is loose; the authors could not prove a bound for the better-performing UCB1-Tuned.
agent_relevance: A stuck search needs an explicit bonus for under-tried branches that shrinks with tries. Cost of exploring a branch is bounded in log terms.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Section 4 experiments
finding: Compared UCB1-Tuned, UCB2 and epsilon_n-greedy on 7 Bernoulli bandits: 2-armed (0.9/0.6, 0.9/0.8, 0.55/0.45) and 10-armed (rows 11-14, e.g. 0.9 vs nine at 0.6). Well-tuned epsilon-greedy almost always did best. UCB1-Tuned was close to it. UCB2 was always slightly worse than UCB1-Tuned.
numbers: 7 reward distributions; easy = large gaps and low variance, hard = small gaps (0.55 vs 0.45). Exceptions where greedy did not win: distributions 12 and 14 (many bad arms with unequal means).
quote: An optimally tuned n-GREEDY performs almost always best.
limits: Epsilon-greedy degrades fast if its parameter is badly tuned (except distribution 13). Choosing the constant needs knowledge of the gap, which is not available in practice. Stationary Bernoulli only.
agent_relevance: Simple random widening works when tuned, but the tuning needs the gap size. A per-class rule should be set from observed pass rates, not a fixed epsilon.

source: Lai and Robbins (1985) Asymptotically efficient adaptive allocation rules
finding: Proved a lower bound: any consistent policy must pull each suboptimal arm at least about ln n over a KL distance times. Showed index policies reach it. Not read this session; described via Auer 2002 and Kaufmann 2012.
numbers: Bound as quoted in Auer 2002 eq. (1): E[T_j(n)] >= (1/D + o(1)) ln n.
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: Gives the price of learning: regret grows at least logarithmically, so some wasted pulls are unavoidable.

source: Thompson (1933) On the likelihood that one unknown probability exceeds another
finding: Origin of Thompson sampling: pick a treatment with the posterior probability that it is best. Motivated by clinical trials with two samples. Not read this session.
numbers: Biometrika 25(3-4):285-294; no figures extracted.
limits: Not opened; bibliographic only.
agent_relevance: Sampling from belief gives exploration that fades by itself as evidence grows.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018/2020) A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling
finding: Explains TS for the Beta-Bernoulli bandit: sample a mean for each arm from its Beta posterior, play the arm with the top sample. Shows greedy can lock onto a bad arm after early luck, while TS keeps probing arms that might be best and skips arms known to be bad.
numbers: Simulation: 3 arms, means 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, uniform prior, 10,000 simulations of 1,000 periods. Greedy does not always converge to arm 1; per-period regret of TS goes to zero, greedy's does not.
quote: the algorithm can get stuck, repeatedly applying a poor action
limits: Tutorial simulation, one setting. Priors matter.
agent_relevance: Greedy lock-in on an early lucky branch is the failure the widen rule must stop. Posterior sampling widens on uncertainty only.

source: Kaufmann, Korda, Munos (2012) Thompson Sampling: an asymptotically optimal finite-time analysis
finding: First proof that TS for Bernoulli bandits matches the Lai-Robbins lower bound, for the uniform prior, with finite-time bounds. Ends a gap where TS was used for years without a proof. Includes numerical comparison with other optimal policies.
numbers: Regret bound of the form (1+eps) * sum (mu*-mu_a)/KL(mu_a,mu*) ln T + C(eps) for Bernoulli arms.
limits: Bernoulli arms and Beta prior; other reward families came in later work.
agent_relevance: TS is not just a heuristic: it is as efficient as the best index rules in the stationary case.

source: Chapelle and Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Showed on simulated and news-recommendation data that TS can beat UCB in practice, which restarted interest in TS. Cited in the Russo tutorial. Not opened.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened; only seen cited in the tutorial (1707.02038).
agent_relevance: Evidence that TS needs no tuned constant, unlike UCB and epsilon-greedy.

source: Kocsis and Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning (UCT)
finding: Applies UCB1 at each tree node to pick which child to expand, giving UCT, the base of Monte-Carlo tree search. Not opened this session.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Direct link to our tree search: each node is a bandit, each child a branch to widen or deepen.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Defines a pseudo-count from any density model over pixels, so count-based bonuses (like UCB's 1/sqrt(N)) work in huge state spaces. Gives much better exploration on hard Atari games including Montezuma's Revenge.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge level 1 has 24 rooms. Full score table could not be parsed reliably, so no scores are recorded here. Burda 2018 says the best earlier methods found about half the rooms.
limits: Bonus is tied to pixel density quality.
agent_relevance: A bonus that decays with visit count is the practical form of UCB for open spaces; a tree needs a similarity measure to count visits to ideas.

source: Pathak, Agrawal, Efros, Darrell (2017) Curiosity-driven exploration by self-supervised prediction
finding: Intrinsic Curiosity Module rewards the agent for error in predicting the next state's features, but only features that the agent's actions can affect (learned via an inverse model). This avoids rewarding unpredictable noise. Tested in VizDoom (sparse and very sparse reward) and Super Mario.
numbers: Noise test: 40% of the visual observation replaced by white noise; ICM still succeeds most of the time, pixel-prediction model struggles. A results table lists success rates TRPO 26.0%, A3C 0.0%, VIME+TRPO 46.1%, ICM+A3C 100.0% (condition not fully parsed).
quote: every state will be novel and it would be impossible to predict the value of any pixel
limits: Only a fixed-region noise distractor tested. Burda 2018 shows a TV the agent can control still hurts.
agent_relevance: Explore only where the agent's own choices change the outcome. Do not reward branches that differ only by sampling noise.

source: Burda, Edwards, Storkey, Klimov (2018/2019) Exploration by random network distillation (RND)
finding: Bonus is the error of a trained network at predicting a fixed random network on the new state. Cheap, no dynamics model, avoids the stochastic-transition trap because the target is deterministic. With no extrinsic reward, the agent finds over half the rooms in Montezuma's Revenge. Needs two value heads (episodic extrinsic, non-episodic intrinsic).
numbers: Pure exploration: non-episodic gamma_I=0.999 explored more rooms than 0.99; one run explored 21 rooms; best return 6,700 in 4 of 5 runs. With rewards: best agent often finds 22 of 24 rooms, occasionally passes level 1. Table 1: Montezuma RND 8,152 vs PPO 2,497 vs dynamics bonus 400; Pitfall! RND -3 (fails, as does PPO); PrivateEye RND 8,666 vs dynamics 105; Venture RND 1,859 vs dynamics 0; Gravitar RND 3,906, PPO 3,426.
limits: Fails on Pitfall!. Gravitar gain over PPO not consistent. Level 1 of Montezuma only rarely passed. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Sparse-reward search needs a separate novelty signal kept apart from the answer signal (two heads). Novelty is a bonus on top of, not a replacement for, the check.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-scale study of curiosity-driven learning
finding: Pure curiosity (no extrinsic reward) trained on 54 environments (Atari, Mario, Roboschool, Unity maze, Pong, etc.). Many games can be played reasonably using only prediction-error bonuses, because game score correlates with novelty. A noisy TV added to a Unity maze drastically slows learning, though agents sometimes still reach the reward given long runs.
numbers: 54 environments. Noisy-TV test in the Unity maze: IDF and random-feature (RF) curiosity both slowed drastically; some agents converge if run long enough.
quote: the presence of the TV drastically slows down learning
limits: Curiosity-only works where the world gives few stochastic distractions; the TV is a thought experiment made literal.
agent_relevance: A widen signal driven by raw diversity or surprise will be hijacked by random variation. Gate any novelty on whether it is reproducible.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2019/2021) Go-Explore
finding: Names two failures of intrinsic-motivation exploration: detachment (agent forgets frontiers it left, after reward dries up there) and derailment (random exploration noise wrecks a return to a promising state). Go-Explore stores an archive of states, returns to a chosen one, then explores from it.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: mean 666,474 with domain knowledge (best run over 18 million, 1,441 levels); mean 43,763 without domain knowledge. Pitfall: mean 59,494, max 107,363 (game max about 112,000). Assumes deterministic training is allowed.
limits: Phase 1 relies on a resettable simulator; strongest results use domain-knowledge cell representation.
agent_relevance: Our tree is an archive. Return to a stored partial solution and expand it, rather than restarting. Matches the idea of keeping best-so-far.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Never Give Up: learning directed exploration strategies
finding: NGU mixes an episodic novelty bonus with a lifelong RND-style bonus, and trains a family of policies from very exploratory to purely greedy that share a network. Aims at hard-exploration games without hurting dense-reward games.
numbers: Per the Agent57 text, NGU still did poorly on some games. Detailed table not parsed.
limits: Skimmed only; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: A spread of explore-heavy to exploit-heavy attempts is the same shape as our mix of typical and untried attempts.

source: Badia et al. (2020) Agent57: outperforming the Atari human benchmark
finding: First deep RL agent above the standard human benchmark on all 57 Atari games. Adds an adaptive meta-controller, a non-stationary multi-armed bandit, that picks which exploration-exploitation policy to run in each episode.
numbers: 57 of 57 games above human; bandit window mean over 50 episodes; text also lists 3,600 episodes and 0.01 as bandit settings.
limits: Window and epsilon are hand-set; the bandit chooses among N pre-made policies, it does not invent new ones. Training scale is large.
agent_relevance: A bandit over modes (direct vs wide search) per problem class is a tested design; use a non-stationary one since class pass rates drift.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 used as bandit agents with the history in the prompt. Only one of many configurations explored well: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought and externally summarized history (counts and means). Others fail by suffix failure (never choose the best arm after some round) or near-uniform play.
numbers: Basic GPT-4 prompt on a 5-armed bandit: suffix failure in over 60% of replicates (like greedy). 32 prompt designs per model; 48 configurations for GPT-3.5 and Llama2 with CoT variants, 72 for GPT-4. Robustness runs: T=200, N=20 and 40 replicates, about 50K GPT-4 queries.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Simple bandits, small T (100 main). Authors use surrogate failure statistics because full regret needs larger T. 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: An LLM left alone does not widen on its own; counts and summaries must be computed by code (matches G5, G12). Raw history in context is not enough.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) prompt-design axes
finding: Prompt design varied on five axes: suggestive framing vs neutral, raw vs summarized history, single arm vs distribution as answer, with or without CoT, plus a reinforced variant for GPT-4. Failing configurations mostly exploit too early; the only success matched Thompson-sampling-like reward.
numbers: 2^5 = 32 prompt designs; the one success is labeled BSSC0 (GPT-4). Compared with epsilon-greedy curves in a suffix-failure versus uniform-failure plane.
limits: Trade-off: configs avoiding suffix failures often play near uniformly (no learning).
agent_relevance: Two failure modes to watch in our agent: collapse onto one branch, and spreading over all branches equally.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration
finding: Benchmarks LLMs on context-free and contextual bandits of varied difficulty. Two fixes: algorithm-guided support (give the LLM UCB-style statistics at inference) and algorithm distillation (train on UCB/TS traces in context or by fine-tuning). Smaller models with these beat larger ones. Fitting cumulative regret: strong settings reach sublinear regret, weak ones (Gemma 2B and 9B) stay linear.
numbers: UCB's optimal-action fraction rises 32.7% to 65.0% over time in one table; fine-tuned Flash models reach sublinear regret with a lower exponent; Gemma 2B/9B remain linear on the Hard setup.
limits: Bandits only; distillation depends on a known algorithm to copy. Gemini and Gemma families mainly.
agent_relevance: Giving the model code-computed UCB scores helps more than model size; supports a code-run widen rule instead of asking the model when to explore.

source: Sutton and Barto (2018) Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, ch. 2 and 8
finding: Standard text defines epsilon-greedy, UCB and gradient bandits, and the exploration bonus in Dyna-Q+ for changing environments. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Dyna-Q+ time-since-tried bonus is an example of a bonus for stale branches.

source: Schmidhuber (2010) Formal theory of creativity, fun, and intrinsic motivation
finding: Source of the white-noise TV example: an agent rewarded for prediction error would stare at noise. Proposes rewarding learning progress (error reduction) instead. Known here via Pathak 2017. Not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened; quoted second-hand.
agent_relevance: Reward progress on the check (it got better), not raw difference.

source: Cross-source synthesis: sparse reward (RND, ICM, Go-Explore)
finding: Across RND, ICM, Large-scale curiosity and Go-Explore, one pattern shows: a plain agent gets no signal where reward is sparse (Pitfall! RND -3, PPO also fails), a novelty bonus gives partial progress (Montezuma 8,152 vs 2,497), and remembering and returning to frontiers gives the largest jump (43,763 mean with no domain knowledge).
numbers: Montezuma means: PPO 2,497; RND 8,152; Go-Explore without domain knowledge 43,763; with 666,474.
limits: Different budgets and training frames across papers; scores not strictly comparable.
agent_relevance: Order of value for our tree: (1) keep an archive and return, (2) novelty bonus, (3) random noise last.

source: Burda et al. (2018) RND ablation: episodic vs non-episodic
finding: Treating game-over as the end of novelty value (episodic) cuts exploration; a non-episodic intrinsic return lets the agent take risks to reach new rooms. Mixing the two streams needs separate value heads and discounts.
numbers: Non-episodic gamma_I=0.999 explored more rooms than 0.99; one run explored 21 rooms. Extrinsic discount 0.99.
limits: Single-game ablation (Montezuma).
agent_relevance: Novelty value should persist across attempts (history kept by code), not reset each try.

source: Auer et al. (2002) UCB1 index definition
finding: UCB1 plays the arm with the highest mean plus sqrt(2 ln n / n_j); each arm is played once first. Because the bonus grows slowly with total time n and shrinks with the arm's own pulls, every arm is revisited at a logarithmic rate.
numbers: The regret bound involves sums of 8 ln n over gap terms plus a constant.
limits: The constant in the bonus comes from Hoeffding for [0,1] rewards; smaller constants do better in practice (UCB1-Tuned).
agent_relevance: Index form is easy to run in code over branch pass counts: no model call needed.

source: Russo et al. (2018) TS tutorial: greedy lock-in mechanism
finding: Greedy settles on arm 3 (mean 0.7) after two early wins, because the untried arms still have expected mean 0.5. TS learns arm 1 in nearly all runs within 1,000 periods. Per-period regret: TS tends to 0; greedy stays above 0.
numbers: Uniform prior; 10,000 simulations, 1,000 steps; arms 0.9, 0.8, 0.7.
limits: Tiny problem; real tasks have more arms and dependence between arms.
agent_relevance: A rule that treats an untried branch as average leads to lock-in. Use optimistic or sampled values for untried classes.

source: RND vs dynamics bonus on the noisy-TV problem
finding: Three fixes to the noisy TV: predict only controllable features (ICM); predict a deterministic random target (RND); reward progress, not error (Schmidhuber). RND's table shows a dynamics-prediction bonus scoring far below RND on several hard games.
numbers: Dynamics bonus vs RND: Montezuma 400 vs 8,152; PrivateEye 105 vs 8,666; Venture 0 vs 1,859.
limits: Authors tie this to stochastic prediction error; other causes not isolated.
agent_relevance: Prefer a deterministic novelty measure. Compute distance in code, not by asking a model if an idea feels new (G8).

source: Agent57 meta-controller as a bandit
finding: Each arm is a (bonus strength, discount) pair. A non-stationary bandit picks an arm per episode and is rewarded with the episode's extrinsic return. The same agent can act explore-heavy on Pitfall and Montezuma and exploit-heavy on dense-reward games.
numbers: Human normalised score above 1 on all 57 games; window mean over 50 episodes.
limits: Hyper-parameters hand-chosen; arms fixed in advance.
agent_relevance: A per-class bandit that picks how wide to search, with a sliding window, gives the per-class widen rule.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) implication: summarize in code
finding: The single working setup gives the LLM sufficient statistics (plays and average reward per arm) computed outside the model, plus CoT. The same model with the raw log fails. The stats step, not the model's reasoning alone, turns exploration on.
numbers: Same GPT-4: raw history gives over 60% suffix failures; summarized plus CoT plus suggestive framing gives very few suffix failures and reward comparable to TS.
limits: Authors note external summarization may not exist for complex tasks.
agent_relevance: Have code keep per-class tries and passes, and feed those counts in or decide widen in code.
